stimulus.source_note: The Colonies Reduced, and Its Companion, designed and engraved for the Political Register, London, December 1768; top image after a 1766 design by Benjamin Franklin (British Museum), public domain.
stimulus.text: This 1768 cartoon, published in London's Political Register, is titled “The Colonies Reduced.” In the top panel, Britannia sits dismembered on the ground, her limbs cut off and labeled Virg., Pensyl., New York, and New Eng.; a ribbon across her body reads “Date Obolum Bellisario” — “Give a penny to Belisarius,” the blinded general reduced to begging. Below, “Its Companion” shows America — a Native American woman — running into the arms of the French king, while Britannia is held back and a Dutchman seizes a British ship.

figures.alt: The Colonies Reduced, 1768 — Britannia dismembered on the ground, her limbs labeled Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, and New England, with France embracing America below
figures.caption: “The Colonies Reduced,” Political Register, London, 1768

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, “The Colonies Reduced” (1768), after Benjamin Franklin, public domain
stem: The lower panel, “Its Companion,” shows America running into the arms of the French king while Britannia is held back and a Dutchman seizes a British ship. Which of the following best explains what the cartoonist is warning British readers about?

options.text: Britain's rivals will profit from the empire's breakup, gaining the trade and power Britain loses.
France has already conquered Britain and now rules the colonies directly.
options.misconception: France has not conquered Britain; the panel shows France hoping to profit, not ruling.

options.text: The colonies have allied with France to destroy the British navy.
options.misconception: There is no colonial-French alliance in 1768; the alliance came a decade later, in 1778.

options.text: Britain should abandon the colonies and concentrate on its European wars instead of defending them.
options.misconception: The cartoon warns against losing the colonies; it does not advise abandoning them.

rationales.A: The lower panel shows America running to the French king, who boasts he will be “King of de whole World,” while a Dutchman seizes a British ship and Britannia is held back. Background: the cartoonist's warning is that a broken empire invites its enemies — the trade, the territory, and the power Britain loses will go straight to France and the other European rivals. The dismemberment above is not just Britain's loss; it is France's opportunity.
rationales.B: France has not conquered Britain; the panel shows France hoping to profit, not ruling.
rationales.C: There is no colonial-French alliance in 1768; the alliance came a decade later, in 1778.
rationales.D: The cartoon warns against losing the colonies; it does not advise abandoning them.
rationales.general:
1. Read the two panels together. Above, Britannia lies in pieces; below, her rivals crowd in.
2. Look at what France is doing. He is not fighting Britain — he is embracing America, who runs to him.
3. Look at the Dutchman. He is seizing a British ship while Britannia is held back.
4. Put it together. The warning is double: Britain is cutting itself apart, and its enemies are waiting to pick up the pieces.
Remember: a cartoon's second panel is its punchline — and this one points at France.
